Sources: miami/AUTHORITY-MAP-MIAMI.md + SPEED-RULES-MIAMI.md + miami/hub.json (v2026-08-15-miami-mece), with PUBLIC-PARTNERS-BRIEF.md patterns. CONTRACT v3: only `title` (≤6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (≤140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Underscore-prefixed fields NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Never render: held corridors, Gulf counterparties, authority contacts, internal dock-status fields. MIAMI SPECIFICS: (1) THE SPEED SECTION IS NOT A RELIEF PITCH — the controlling regime is manatee protection (animal-strike prevention, not wake control); every posted zone is respected as-is, corridor times already reflect them, and NO exemption is sought, claimed, or implied anywhere. The `speed_rule_relief` key is retained ONLY for template compatibility; it contains compliance-and-routing content, relief_minutes is null, there is no Stockholm precedent line, and the 'What relief unlocks' layer must NOT render for Miami. (2) Classification dual, Enable-weighted; the Operate flavor is municipal purchase-of-service (Miami Beach free water taxi, LauderGO! Water Trolley, Pompano Beach), not agency fleet ownership — no public vessel-owning operator exists here and DTPW has no verified water program. (3) The 2024 paid water-taxi pilot was a City of Miami Beach program, correctly attributed; its contracted operator is never named on renderables. (4) Bodies with unverified posture (Broward County, City of Hollywood, Aventura/Sunny Isles, Village of Key Biscayne, FDOT District Four, USACE) are omitted, as are the five landings lacking document-level ownership verification from any claims. (5) Two independent networks — no Miami–Fort Lauderdale water link. (6) Hub gates banned terms respected on all renderables.

copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice. South Florida leans Enable, and its Operate track is one your cities already use: purchase-of-service. Cities here already buy water transit by the month.
copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing marinas and park docks and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; privately committed employer demand fills the seats. The ask is access, not money.
copy.operate_track: Miami Beach, Fort Lauderdale, and Pompano Beach all pay private operators to run scheduled water service today. Navier service can be procured the same way — by contract, by the month — to build or extend a public water network.

copy.headline: We schedule around the manatee zones — as written.
copy.framing: The controlling speed rules on these waters are manatee protection zones. They exist to protect animals, not to manage wake — so we claim no exemption from them, anywhere. Every corridor time on this page respects every posted zone as-is.
copy.ask: Where the rules allow speed, the water is already fast: much of Biscayne Bay's transit water is open bay or posted 25–35 mph channel — at or near foil cruise speed. Our advantage comes from routing and quiet electric operation, not from exemptions.

data.controlling_regime: FWC manatee protection zones (Miami-Dade and Broward) and federal slow-speed water at the Port of Miami

expander.title: How the schedule respects the zones
body: Speed zones on Biscayne Bay and the Intracoastal are set by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission to prevent vessel strikes on manatees. A low-wake hull does not change that purpose — so no exemption is sought, claimed, or modeled, and every posted zone binds our schedule as-is.

The honest advantage here is geography. Large parts of Biscayne Bay's transit water are open bay or numeric 25–35 mph channels — at or near foil cruise speed. Corridors are routed around restricted water, including the year-round no-entry area west of Virginia Key and the slow federal water at the Port of Miami entrance.

Where the zones bind, the schedule bends. The Aventura landing runs summer season only, because its Intracoastal channel is a slow-speed manatee zone from November 15 to April 30 — and Fort Lauderdale's river and port waters are scheduled at their posted slow speeds all year.

_provenance.doctrine: SPEED-RULES-MIAMI.md standing honesty rule (supersedes the generic §4b relief pillar): manatee zones are animal-strike prevention, not wake control; foil-strut strike risk at speed is an open, unstudied question; NO relief case is made or implied for any manatee zone. The Port of Miami RNA and the 2025 Lauderdale Beach restricted area are safety/congestion rules — a low-wake argument does not serve their purposes either; no exemption pathway is claimed for them.

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for shared waterways and shoreline neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 20 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: South Florida's water-transportation landscape spans county, state, regional, and municipal bodies. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.body: Miami-Dade County Parks, Recreation and Open Spaces
bodies.role: Operates the county marina system; Crandon Park, Pelican Harbor, and Bill Bird (Haulover) marinas host three of the network's landings.
Owns and operates Dinner Key Marina — Florida's largest wet-slip marina — and Miamarina at Bayside, two landings on this network.
Runs a free commuter water taxi across Biscayne Bay through a contracted operator; owns the Maurice Gibb Park dock and the land under Miami Beach Marina.
Owns New River Downtown Docking and the land under Bahia Mar, and funds the free LauderGO! Water Trolley — a live purchase-of-service precedent.
Hosts Water Taxi service at its own Alsdorf Park dock — the Fort Lauderdale line's northern landing is already a water-transit stop.
The county's transit operator (Metrorail, Metromover, Metrobus) — the natural integration partner for connections and fares.
State transportation district for Miami-Dade — steward of the congested causeway corridors this network parallels.
Regional planning and funding channel; its Mobility Hubs program put a fully federally funded hub in downtown Fort Lauderdale.
County seaport department; a consultation stakeholder for transits near Government Cut — no network landing sits on port property.
County environmental regulator for Biscayne Bay; environmental permits apply to any landing modification.
Biscayne Bay is a state aquatic preserve; submerged-lands authorizations apply to structural changes. Existing berths used as-is minimize exposure.

bodies.body: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC)
bodies.role: Sets and enforces the manatee protection zones that govern vessel speed on these waters — rules this network respects as written.
Federal navigation-safety authority; slow-speed water at the Port of Miami entrance channels binds the Beach line's marina exit.
